title: Unit 6: Integration and Accumulation of Change

topics.name: Accumulated change and Riemann sums
covers: Using definite integrals to determine accumulated change over an interval

guide.title: Integration and accumulation of change: review guide
guide.intro: A definite integral adds up a rate of change to give the total change. This unit approximates integrals with sums, connects them to antiderivatives through the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, and builds the BC integration techniques: substitution, integration by parts, partial fractions, and improper integrals.

sections.title: Accumulated change and Riemann sums
body: If r(t) is a rate, ∫ from a to b of r(t) dt is the net amount accumulated from t = a to t = b, in units of (rate units) × (time units). Starting amount + the integral of the rate = the ending amount.

A Riemann sum adds rectangle areas: (height) × (width) for each subinterval. Left and right sums use the function's value at each subinterval's left or right end; a trapezoidal sum averages them. The widths may be unequal when the data come from a table.
points: For an increasing function, a left sum underestimates and a right sum overestimates.
Use each subinterval's own width when the table's spacing is uneven.
Area below the axis counts as negative in a definite integral.

sections.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and antiderivatives
body: FTC part 1: if g(x) = ∫ from a to x of f(t) dt, then g′(x) = f(x). With a function as the upper limit, use the chain rule: d/dx ∫ from a to u(x) of f(t) dt = f(u(x))·u′(x).
FTC part 2: ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a), where F′ = f. An indefinite integral ∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + C names the whole family of antiderivatives.
points: Don't forget + C on an indefinite integral.
The lower limit's constant disappears when you differentiate an accumulation function.
Basic antiderivatives reverse the derivative rules: ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C for n ≠ −1, and ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + C.

sections.title: Integration techniques and improper integrals
body: Substitution (u-sub) reverses the chain rule: choose u so that du appears in the integrand. Integration by parts reverses the product rule: ∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du. Partial fractions split a rational function with distinct linear factors into simpler fractions that integrate to logarithms.

An improper integral has an infinite limit or an integrand that becomes unbounded. Write it as a limit, such as ∫ from 1 to ∞ = lim b→∞ ∫ from 1 to b, and evaluate the limit: if it is finite, the integral converges.
points: For parts, choose u to get simpler when differentiated (often a polynomial).
∫ from 1 to ∞ of 1/xᵖ dx converges for p > 1 and diverges for p ≤ 1.
An unbounded integrand can still have a finite integral, as with 1/√x on [0, 1].

example.solution: Use parts with u = x and dv = eˣ dx, so du = dx and v = eˣ. Then ∫ x eˣ dx = x eˣ − ∫ eˣ dx = x eˣ − eˣ + C = eˣ(x − 1) + C. Check: the derivative is eˣ + x eˣ − eˣ = x eˣ.

misconceptions: “A definite integral is always an area, so it's never negative.”
It's a net (signed) total; parts below the axis subtract.
“d/dx ∫ from 0 to x³ of f(t) dt = f(x³).”
With a function as the upper limit, multiply by its derivative: f(x³)·3x².
“If the integrand blows up, the integral diverges.”
Evaluate the limit: some unbounded integrands have finite integrals.
“∫ f(x)g(x) dx = ∫ f(x) dx · ∫ g(x) dx.”
Integrals don't split over products; use substitution or parts.

questions.prompt: Water flows into a tank at r(t) gallons per minute, where t is in minutes. What does ∫ from 0 to 10 of r(t) dt represent?
choices: The rate of flow at t = 10 minutes
The amount of water in the tank at t = 10 minutes
The total gallons that flow into the tank during the first 10 minutes
The average rate of flow during the first 10 minutes
questions.explanation: Integrating a rate over a time interval gives the total change: gallons per minute × minutes = gallons that entered from t = 0 to t = 10.
choiceExplanations: r(10) is the rate at t = 10; the integral adds up the rate over the whole interval.
The tank's amount at t = 10 also includes whatever was in it at t = 0.
The average rate would be the integral divided by 10.

questions.prompt: A table gives f(0) = 4, f(2) = 6, f(5) = 3, and f(9) = 5. Using a left Riemann sum with the three subintervals the table gives, what is the approximation of ∫ from 0 to 9 of f(x) dx?
choiceExplanations: 41 is the right Riemann sum (6·2 + 3·3 + 5·4).
39 uses a width of 3 for every subinterval, but the widths are 2, 3, and 4.
39.5 is the trapezoidal sum.

questions.prompt: A tank holds 50 liters at t = 0. Water leaks out at r(t) = 2t liters per minute for 0 ≤ t ≤ 5. How much water is in the tank at t = 5?
questions.explanation: The amount leaked is ∫ from 0 to 5 of 2t dt = 25 liters, so 50 − 25 = 25 liters remain.
choiceExplanations: 40 subtracts the rate at t = 5 (10 L/min), not the total leaked.
75 adds the leaked amount instead of subtracting it.
0 assumes the leak rate stays at its maximum, 10 L/min, for all 5 minutes.

questions.prompt: What is d/dx ∫ from 1 to x of cos(t²) dt?
questions.explanation: By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, the derivative of ∫ from a to x of f(t) dt is f(x), so the answer is cos(x²).
choiceExplanations: sin(x²) treats the problem as finding an antiderivative.
The upper limit is x, whose derivative is 1, so there is no factor 2x.
The constant lower limit contributes nothing to the derivative.

questions.prompt: What is d/dx ∫ from 0 to x³ of √(1 + t) dt?
questions.explanation: FTC with the chain rule: f(x³)·(x³)′ = √(1 + x³)·3x².
choiceExplanations: 3x²√(1 + x) evaluates the integrand at x instead of at x³.
√(1 + x³) forgets to multiply by the derivative of the upper limit.
The lower limit is a constant, so nothing is subtracted.

questions.prompt: What is ∫ from 0 to 2 of (3x² − 2x) dx?
questions.explanation: An antiderivative is x³ − x², so the integral is (8 − 4) − 0 = 4.
choiceExplanations: 12 adds the two parts (8 + 4) instead of subtracting.
8 is the integrand's value at x = 2, not the integral.
0 uses 2x² as the antiderivative of 2x.

questions.explanation: Let u = x², so du = 2x dx and x dx = du/2. Then ∫ eᵘ du/2 = (1/2)eᵘ + C = (1/2)e^(x²) + C.
choiceExplanations: Its derivative is 2x e^(x²), twice the integrand.
This integrates x and e^(x²) separately and multiplies, which isn't valid.
Its derivative is 4x e^(x²), four times the integrand.

questions.prompt: What is ∫ x cos x dx?
choices: x sin x − cos x + C
x sin x + cos x + C
questions.explanation: Parts with u = x, dv = cos x dx: du = dx, v = sin x. So ∫ x cos x dx = x sin x − ∫ sin x dx = x sin x + cos x + C.
choiceExplanations: Integrals don't split over products: the derivative of (x²/2) sin x isn't x cos x.
∫ sin x dx = −cos x, so subtracting it gives + cos x, not − cos x.
The sign of x sin x is wrong: v = ∫ cos x dx = +sin x.

choiceExplanations: Its derivative is 1/(x − 1) + 1/(x + 2), which isn't the integrand.
This has the wrong sign: it's the negative of the answer.
The coefficients are 1/3, not 3.

questions.prompt: What is ∫ from 1 to ∞ of 1/x² dx?
questions.explanation: lim b→∞ ∫ from 1 to b of x⁻² dx = lim b→∞ (1 − 1/b) = 1. It converges because p = 2 > 1.
choiceExplanations: −1 subtracts in the wrong order: the antiderivative −1/x goes from −1 at x = 1 up to 0, a change of +1.
The integrand is positive, so the integral can't be 0.
1/xᵖ integrals from 1 to ∞ converge when p > 1; here p = 2.

questions.prompt: What is ∫ from 0 to 1 of 1/√x dx?
choices: It diverges, because 1/√x is unbounded near 0
questions.explanation: lim a→0⁺ ∫ from a to 1 of x^(−1/2) dx = lim a→0⁺ (2 − 2√a) = 2. The integrand is unbounded, but the area is finite.
choiceExplanations: An unbounded integrand doesn't automatically mean divergence; the limit here is finite.
1/2 multiplies by the exponent instead of dividing by the new exponent 1/2.
1 forgets the factor 2 in the antiderivative 2√x.
